title: ctags: the original index
description: ctags scans source files with regex-like parsers and emits a tags file — name, file, pattern — that editors use for jump-to-definition. It is dumb but universal: 40+ languages, no build needed, works on any codebase in seconds. Every fancier system (LSP, code search) still falls back to ctags-shaped indexes when deep analysis is unavailable.
mechanism: Per-language parsers scan for definition patterns (function/class/variable); emit sorted tags file; editor binary-searches it. Exuberant/Universal Ctags added kinds, roles, and JSON output.
algo: O(n) scan per file; O(log tags) lookup by binary search. No type information — name-based only.
demo:
import re

src = '''def search(q):
    pass

class Index:
    def add(self, doc):
        pass
'''
# ctags-style: regex parsers per language, emitting (name, kind, line)
tags = []
for i, line in enumerate(src.splitlines(), 1):
    m = re.match(r'\s*(?:def|class)\s+(\w+)', line)
    if m:
        tags.append((m.group(1), 'def' if line.strip().startswith('def') else 'class', i))
tags.sort()
print('tags file:')
for name, kind, line in tags:
    print('  %-8s %-5s line %d' % (name, kind, line))
print('jump-to-definition = binary search this file (no build, no types)')

title: LSP references
description: The Language Server Protocol turned cross-referencing into a commodity: textDocument/references asks the server for every use of the symbol under the cursor, and the server answers from its index. Because the server parses with full type information, results are precise — overrides, implementations, and references distinguished — not the name-matches ctags returns.
mechanism: Server maintains a reference index (symbol -> locations) updated incrementally; references request returns them with context. Declaration vs definition vs implementation are separate requests.
algo: O(1) lookup in the reference index; O(changed) incremental updates. Precision from type-aware analysis.

title: Call graphs
description: A call graph links every caller to every callee — the map of how control flows through the program. Static call graphs are built from the AST with class-hierarchy or points-to analysis for dynamic dispatch; dynamic ones from execution traces. They power 'who calls this', dead-code detection, and impact analysis: change a function, see every path that reaches it.
mechanism: For each call site, resolve targets: direct calls trivially, method calls via class hierarchy (CHA) or points-to sets (Andersen). Edges = (caller, callee). Dynamic: instrument and record.
algo: CHA is O(program); Andersen points-to is O(n^3) worst case, near-linear in practice. Dynamic is O(executed calls).
demo:
import ast

src = '''def a():
    b()
    c()
def b():
    c()
def c():
    pass
a()
'''
tree = ast.parse(src)

class CG(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def __init__(self):
        self.cur, self.edges = None, []
    def visit_FunctionDef(self, node):
        self.cur = node.name
        self.generic_visit(node)
        self.cur = None
    def visit_Call(self, node):
        if isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and self.cur:
            self.edges.append((self.cur, node.func.id))
        self.generic_visit(node)

cg = CG()
cg.visit(tree)
print('call edges:', cg.edges)
# who calls c? reverse the edges
callers = sorted({a for a, b in cg.edges if b == 'c'})
print('callers of c:', callers, '(impact analysis: change c, check these)')

title: Def-use chains
description: Def-use chains connect each variable definition to every use it can reach — the fine-grained truth behind rename refactoring and dataflow analysis. Built by walking the control-flow graph with reaching-definitions analysis: a definition reaches a use if some path carries it there without an intervening redefinition. Rename is safe exactly when the chain is complete.
mechanism: CFG + reaching definitions (dataflow fixpoint): IN/OUT sets per block. Chain: for each use, the definitions in the reaching set. SSA form makes chains explicit: each variable assigned once, phi-nodes merge.
algo: Reaching definitions is O(blocks * vars) per fixpoint iteration; SSA construction is O(n).

title: Cross-repo xrefs
description: Monorepos and multi-repo systems need references that cross repository boundaries: the Python client calling the Go service's API. Cross-repo xref indexes each repo's symbols into a shared schema (name, kind, repo, file, line) and resolves by fully-qualified name. The hard part is versioning — repo A at commit X references repo B at commit Y — so the index is version-aware.
mechanism: Per-repo symbol extraction -> shared index keyed by qualified name + repo@version. References resolve against the pinned versions in the lockfile/manifest. Stale pins produce 'definition moved' hints, not silent misses.
algo: O(repos * symbols) indexing; O(1) qualified lookup. Version pinning keeps results reproducible.

title: Symbol servers
description: A symbol server centralizes the index: developers' editors query it instead of each building their own. It ingests repos on commit, extracts symbols incrementally, and serves definition/reference queries over HTTP. The economics are clear at scale — parse once centrally, serve thousands of editors — and it enables cross-repo features no single editor index could offer.
mechanism: Ingest pipeline: on push, parse changed files, update the symbol DB. Query API: symbol search, definitions, references with repo@version scoping. Cache hot queries; shard the index by repo.
algo: Ingest O(changed files) per push; queries O(1) indexed. Parse-once-serve-many amortizes cost over all developers.

title: Dependency graphs
description: Dependency graphs map module-to-module imports — the architecture made visible. Cycles in the graph are design smells (A imports B imports A); the graph's layers reveal whether the architecture matches the intent. Tools extract imports statically per file and render the graph; CI fails on new cycles or on layering violations (UI importing the database layer directly).
mechanism: Parse imports per file (AST for Python, import statements elsewhere); nodes = modules, edges = imports. Detect cycles with DFS coloring; enforce layering with allowed-edge rules.
algo: O(files + imports) extraction; O(V+E) cycle detection. Layering checks are edge-rule lookups.

title: Impact analysis
description: Impact analysis answers 'if I change this, what breaks?' by traversing the call and dependency graphs from the changed symbol. Forward traversal finds affected callers and dependents; combined with test mapping (which tests cover which code), it selects the minimal test set to run. It turns 'run the whole suite to be safe' into 'run these 40 tests'.
mechanism: Build call graph + reverse edges (callee -> callers). From the changed symbol, BFS the reverse graph to find all transitive callers. Intersect with the test-coverage map to pick tests.
algo: BFS over reverse call graph: O(affected). Test selection is a set intersection.

title: Rename refactoring
description: Rename looks trivial and is anything but: every reference must move, including dynamic ones (getattr, string references, config files). Safe rename needs complete def-use chains plus heuristics for the dynamic cases, applied as one atomic edit with preview. The IDE shows every occurrence; the user confirms; the tool rewrites. A rename that misses one dynamic reference is a runtime bug.
mechanism: Resolve the symbol's def-use chain; find textual matches as candidates; classify each (certain reference / possible dynamic / unrelated same-name); rewrite certain ones, flag possible ones for review. Preview diff before applying.
algo: O(references) rewrite. Dynamic-reference heuristics are the precision/recall tradeoff.
demo:
import ast, re

src = 'total = 0\ndef get_total():\n    return total\nprint(total)\nprint(getattr(obj, "total"))\n'
tree = ast.parse(src)

certain = [(n.lineno, 'static') for n in ast.walk(tree)
           if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and n.id == 'total']
dynamic = [(i + 1, 'dynamic?') for i, l in enumerate(src.splitlines()) if '"total"' in l]
print('certain references (AST):', certain)
print('possible dynamic (string):', dynamic, '-> flagged for human review')
new = re.sub(r'\btotal\b', 'grand_total', src)
print('--- after rename ---')
print(new)

title: Dead code detection
description: Dead code is unreachable from any entry point: functions nobody calls, branches never taken, imports never used. Detection starts from entry points (main, tests, exported APIs) and marks reachable symbols through the call graph; unmarked exported-or-internal symbols are candidates. Dynamic languages need care — reflection and plugins create invisible edges, so production tools combine static reachability with coverage data.
mechanism: Entry points -> BFS over call graph -> reachable set. Candidates = all definitions - reachable - exported API. Confirm with coverage: never-executed candidates are almost certainly dead.
algo: O(program) reachability. Coverage confirmation needs a test run.
demo:
import ast

src = '''def used():
    return 1
def unused():
    return 2
print(used())
'''
tree = ast.parse(src)
defs = {n.name for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef)}
called = {n.func.id for n in ast.walk(tree)
          if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name)}
# entry: module top-level calls; reachable = called (1-level here; real tools do full BFS)
dead = defs - called
print('defined:', defs)
print('called :', called)
print('dead candidates:', dead, '(confirm with coverage before deleting)')

title: Incremental xref updates
description: Rebuilding the cross-reference index on every keystroke is impossible at scale — updates must be incremental. The index stores per-file symbol tables; on edit, only that file's entries are recomputed and merged. References from other files to changed symbols are patched via the reverse index. The invariant: the index always reflects the current buffer contents, with per-file granularity.
mechanism: Per-file symbol records with content hashes; on change, re-extract that file, diff against old records, apply deltas to the global index and reverse map. Batch rapid keystrokes with a debounce.
algo: O(changed file) per update; global structures patched by delta, never rebuilt.
demo:
import ast, hashlib

index, hashes = {}, {}  # symbol -> locations; file -> content hash

def reindex(path, src):
    h = hashlib.md5(src.encode()).hexdigest()
    if hashes.get(path) == h:
        return 'unchanged: skip'
    hashes[path] = h
    # remove old entries from this file
    for sym in [s for s, locs in index.items() if any(l[0] == path for l in locs)]:
        index[sym] = [l for l in index[sym] if l[0] != path]
    for n in ast.walk(ast.parse(src)):
        if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef):
            index.setdefault(n.name, []).append((path, n.lineno))
    return 'rebuilt %s only' % path

print(reindex('a.py', 'def f():\n    pass\n'))
print(reindex('a.py', 'def f():\n    pass\n'))  # same content: skipped
print(reindex('a.py', 'def f():\n    pass\ndef g():\n    pass\n'))
print('index:', index)

title: Xref accuracy: precision vs recall
description: Cross-reference tools trade precision (every reported reference is real) against recall (every real reference is reported). Name-based tools (ctags) have high recall and low precision — they match same-named unrelated symbols. Type-aware tools (LSP) have both high, at the cost of full analysis. The right choice depends on the task: rename needs precision; exploration tolerates noise.
mechanism: Measure against ground truth (manually verified references on a corpus): precision = true/(true+false), recall = true/(true+missed). Improve precision with type filtering; improve recall with dynamic-reference heuristics.
algo: Evaluation is O(reported + truth). The tradeoff curve guides which engine backs which feature.
demo:
# name-based vs type-aware: precision/recall on overloaded method names
# truth: 3 real refs to A.save, 2 same-named B.save (different class)
truth = {'a.py:10', 'a.py:22', 'b.py:5'}
name_based = {'a.py:10', 'a.py:22', 'b.py:5', 'c.py:8', 'c.py:9'}  # ctags: matches B.save too
type_aware = {'a.py:10', 'a.py:22', 'b.py:5'}                     # LSP: resolves the class

def pr(reported):
    tp = len(reported & truth)
    return tp / len(reported), tp / len(truth)

print('name-based: P=%.2f R=%.2f (noisy)' % pr(name_based))
print('type-aware: P=%.2f R=%.2f (precise)' % pr(type_aware))
print('rename needs precision; exploration tolerates noise')

title: Code navigation UX
description: The best index is useless with bad UX: navigation must be instant (<100ms), show context (a few lines around each reference), and support peek-without-leaving (inline preview). Breadcrumb trails show where you are; back/forward navigates the jump history. The research is clear — developers navigate constantly, and every 500ms of latency measurably reduces exploration.
mechanism: Jump stack (back/forward), peek windows (inline reference list), breadcrumbs from the scope chain. All backed by the same index; the UX is a view layer over O(1) lookups.
algo: UX-level: O(1) index lookups; the latency budget is rendering, not search.
demo:
# jump stack: every go-to-definition pushes; back/forward pops
stack, forward = [], []
loc = ('main.py', 1)

def goto(f, line):
    global loc
    stack.append(loc)
    forward.clear()
    loc = (f, line)
    print('jump -> %s:%d' % (f, line))

def back():
    global loc
    if stack:
        forward.append(loc)
        loc = stack.pop()
        print('back -> %s:%d' % loc)

goto('index.py', 42)
goto('store.py', 17)
back()
print('peek: show references inline without leaving; breadcrumbs from scope chain')

title: Xrefs at monorepo scale
description: At monorepo scale (millions of files), no single machine holds the index — it shards by directory subtree, with a query fan-out layer merging results. Freshness comes from the build graph: file changes trigger re-indexing of exactly the affected shards. Google's Kythe and Sourcegraph run this architecture: per-shard indexes, merged at query time, updated incrementally off the build.
mechanism: Shard by path prefix; build system emits compilation units; indexers consume them into per-shard stores; query layer fans out and merges. Stale shards are versioned out, never half-updated.
algo: Index O(files) distributed; query O(shards) fan-out merged in O(results log results).

title: Semantic code search
description: Semantic code search finds code by meaning, not text: 'retry with backoff' matches implementations that never use those words. It embeds functions (AST-aware models) and searches by vector similarity, then re-ranks with the xref index (prefer definitions over copies, prefer used code over dead). The combination — semantic recall plus structural precision — beats either alone.
mechanism: Embed every function (code model); ANN index over embeddings; query embedded the same way; re-rank hits by xref signals (reference count, centrality). Hybrid with keyword search for exact names.
algo: ANN over function embeddings; re-rank O(candidates). Xref signals computed from the static index.
